You are comparing two drafts written from the same brief. Read no other file, and do not run commands or browse; judge only the text below.

Brief: Write the README's opening paragraph and its Install and update section for the `tidy-hooks` plugin.

<<<DRAFT A
`tidy-hooks` is a Claude and Codex plugin that blocks `git commit` when staged files contain merge markers. The hook fails open: if Node.js is missing, commits proceed.

## Install and update

### Claude

Install:

```sh
claude plugin marketplace add example/tidy
claude plugin install tidy-hooks@tidy
```

Update:

```sh
claude plugin update tidy-hooks@tidy
```

### Codex

Install:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace add example/tidy
codex plugin add tidy-hooks@tidy
```

Codex skips plugin hooks until you review and trust them.

Update:

```sh
codex plugin marketplace upgrade tidy
```

Then restart Codex.
DRAFT A>>>

items.title: Thinking
items.text:
I'm comparing the two versions: A explains "fails open" right after using it, while B drops the term but keeps its meaning. I'm also weighing where the Codex trust note belongs. It applies after installing, but placing it earlier warns the reader sooner, and A's spot after install and before update fits where the trust step actually comes up.

I'm weighing the two versions on the reader's side: B spells out the steps and puts the trust note before install, while A is more consistent in its wording. I'm leaning toward A overall, since B's extra phrasing adds little.

{"reader": "SAME", "careful": "A", "overall": "A", "reason": "Both drafts give the same commands, and a first-time reader can follow either one, but A uses parallel 'Install:'/'Update:' labels throughout, whereas B shifts between 'To update:' and 'To update, run:' and adds step text that only repeats what the commands already show."}
